From classroom to career: Strengthening professional growth for teachers
item.description:
Teachers are often called the builders of a nation. In Bangladesh, this respect for teachers is deeply rooted in our society. Almost everyone has a teacher they remember someone who encouraged them, guided them or helped shape their future.
But behind this respect is a profession that still faces many challenges. For many teachers, access to quality training remains limited. Career growth is not always clear, and opportunities to improve professional skills often depend on where they work or the resources available to them.
When we discuss education reform, our conversations usually focus on students, textbooks, examinations and curriculum changes. These issues are important, but there is another question we must ask: how are we supporting the people who make education possible?
World Teachers’ Day, observed on October 5, gives us a chance to think about this. This year also marks 60 years since the adoption of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers, which highlighted the importance of teacher preparation, professional development, rights and working conditions.
The message remains relevant today. A good education system is not built only through policies and infrastructure. It depends largely on the teachers who stand in classrooms every day.
Every successful professional begins with a teacher. Doctors, engineers, entrepreneurs, researchers and public servants all carry lessons they learned from their teachers. The quality of education, therefore, depends greatly on whether teachers themselves receive opportunities to learn and grow.
Teaching is a respected profession, but respect alone is not enough to build a sustainable career. Like professionals in other fields, teachers need proper training, recognition and a clear path for advancement.
Many teachers in Bangladesh still struggle to find that path. A young teacher entering the profession may not always know what opportunities are available after gaining classroom experience. Can they become a senior teacher, academic coordinator, school leader or trainer? What qualifications will help them move forward? In many cases, these questions remain unanswered.
Training opportunities also vary widely. Some teachers have access to workshops, courses and mentoring, while others may have limited opportunities because of location, institutional support or financial challenges.
This affects how young graduates view teaching as a career. Many compares teaching with sectors such as technology, banking, multinational companies and development organizations, where career progression and professional learning systems are often more structured.
If we want talented young people to choose teaching and remain in the profession, we need to create stronger opportunities for growth.
This is not only a challenge for Bangladesh. Countries around the world are facing teacher shortages and difficulties in attracting and retaining skilled educators. According to UNESCO, millions of additional teachers will be needed globally by 2030.
This global demand also shows the changing role of teachers. Today’s teachers need more than subject knowledge. Skills in classroom management, lesson planning, assessment, educational technology and child development are becoming increasingly important.
For Bangladeshi teachers, developing these skills can create opportunities both within the country and internationally.
However, teachers who wish to work abroad need to understand that requirements differ from country to country. There is no single qualification that guarantees a teaching position everywhere. Academic background, teaching experience, professional training, language skills and licensing requirements all play a role.
The Gulf countries, including the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, have become destinations for many international teachers. Their international schools often follow British, American, IB and other curricula. Teachers applying for these positions usually need relevant degrees, teaching experience, professional qualifications and good communication skills.
Europe offers opportunities as well, but the process can be more complicated. In many countries, teaching is a regulated profession. Foreign qualifications may need assessment, additional certification or local language skills.
England also has specific requirements for overseas-trained teachers. While some teachers may work in certain situations without immediately obtaining Qualified Teacher Status (QTS), it remains an important qualification for many long-term teaching careers.
Therefore, teachers should research carefully before choosing professional qualifications or planning an international career.
For English-language teachers, qualifications such as Cambridge’s Teaching Knowledge Test (TKT) can support professional learning by improving understanding of teaching methods, lesson planning and classroom practices. However, it should be seen as a professional development qualification, not a universal teaching license.
Teachers working with young children can also benefit from Early Childhood Development (ECD) training. Understanding child behavior, learning through play, classroom safety and child development is essential for effective early-years education.
Learning should not stop when a teacher enters the classroom. In many ways, teaching itself is a lifelong learning profession.
Bangladesh needs more accessible ways for teachers to continue developing their skills. Training should not be something available only to a few; it should become a regular part of every teacher’s professional journey.
Workshops, mentoring programmes, online courses, teacher networks and recognized certifications can help create more learning opportunities.
Private initiatives can also play a role. Platforms such as Teachers Time provide training opportunities in areas including English-language teaching, Early Childhood Development, classroom management, child development and project-based learning.
Such platforms cannot replace universities or formal teacher-training institutions, but they can support teachers who may not otherwise have easy access to professional learning.
Building a stronger teacher-development system requires cooperation among schools, universities, government agencies, development organisations and education technology companies.
Different teachers need different kinds of support. A mathematics teacher may want to improve assessment techniques. An English teacher may seek international teaching qualifications. An early-years educator may need deeper knowledge of child psychology. A school leader may require training in management and leadership.
Professional development should become a natural part of teaching, not something teachers have to discover on their own.
On World Teachers’ Day, we often remember the teachers who influenced our lives. That appreciation matters, but teachers need more than appreciation.
They need opportunities to grow.
A young teacher starting a career in Dhaka, Chattogram, Rajshahi, Khulna or a rural school should be able to see a future ahead — becoming a senior teacher, curriculum specialist, school leader, teacher trainer or international educator.
Sixty years after the ILO/UNESCO recommendation, Bangladesh has an opportunity to rethink how teachers are supported. The question is not only whether we respect teachers, but whether we provide them with the tools, training and opportunities they need to build meaningful careers.
If we want better education outcomes, investing in teachers must be at the heart of that effort.
Tahmina Rahman is an author, teacher trainer of Teachers Time. She can be reached at tahmina.sathi90@gmail.com

India opposition leaders briefly detained in election protest
item.description:
India’s opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained by police on Tuesday during a march protesting against the Election Commission, demanding its chief resign and alleging wrongdoing during a revision of voter rolls.
An AFP reporter saw Gandhi, a leader of the Congress Party, standing on a police barricade and waving an Indian flag. Officers detained him briefly, along with other lawmakers, and then released them soon after.
Opposition parties began their march from parliament towards to the Election Commission of India (ECI), but were stopped by heavy police deployments. Some politicians sat down on the street to wait.
Protests began on Friday, demanding that commission chief Gyanesh Kumar step down.
Opposition politicians have accused the commission of acting at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
The ECI has rejected allegations of wrongdoing, saying the revision process is aimed at ensuring the accuracy and integrity of electoral rolls.
Kumar has not commented publicly.
“Gyanesh, it’s done, bro,” placards read, as well as signs alleging electoral manipulation.
Opposition leaders pressed their demands for greater transparency in the revision of voter lists, alleging that changes to the rolls could disenfranchise eligible voters.
The protest was part of a wider campaign against the Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.
The issue of voter deletion was reignited by a report in September by The Indian Express newspaper, which said two of the ECI’s three members had formally objected at least 14 times to key decisions linked to the voter roll revision.
The news report claimed the names of 130 million citizens had been deleted since the exercise began in 2025.

item.title: PM joins Children’s Rights Day, Shishu Academy’s 50th anniversary event
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Tuesday joined a program marking Children’s Rights Day 2026 and the 50th anniversary of Bangladesh Shishu Academy.
The three-day observance is being held at Bangladesh Shishu Academy in the capital from October 6 to 8, with this year’s theme “Let every child have a secure future.”
Around 150 children welcomed the prime minister upon his arrival at the venue in the morning.
The event began with the national anthem, after which the prime minister took his seat alongside other guests.
Prime minister’s wife and Ziaur Rahman Foundation Vice-Chairman Dr Zubaida Rahman were present at the program, chaired by Women and Children Affairs Minister Prof Dr AZM Zahid Hossain.
The program features a cultural performance by children, presentation of commemorative gifts to children and the unveiling of the souvenir titled Shaishab.
The prime minister is also scheduled to interact with children from different parts of the country through a videoconference.
He will also visit an exhibition featuring paintings by children and a photo gallery.
After the program, the prime minister will visit the Children’s Museum building and inaugurate a solar panel system and a substation on its ground floor.

item.title: Dengue cases surge in Chittagong, 21 deaths recorded this year
item.description:
The dengue outbreak in Chittagong is intensifying, with 4,914 infections and 21 deaths recorded in the district between January 1 and October 5.
The situation worsened sharply in September, when 2,430 cases and 16 deaths were reported.
According to the District Civil Surgeon’s Office, 107 new dengue cases were detected in the 24 hours until 8am on Sunday. Of the 4,914 patients recorded this year, 260 are currently undergoing treatment at different hospitals, while 4,654 have recovered and been discharged.
The dengue situation remained relatively mild at the beginning of the year, with 68 cases in January, 22 in February, 20 in March, 29 in April and 37 in May.
Cases began rising in June, reaching 122 that month, followed by 536 in July and 1,202 in August. The number surged to 2,430 in September.
Another 448 cases were reported in the first five days of October.
September was also the deadliest month, accounting for 16 of the 21 deaths recorded this year. Two deaths each were reported in July and August, while one was recorded in February.
No new dengue deaths were reported in the 24 hours preceding the latest update.
According to data from the District Civil Surgeon’s Office, 2,285 of the 4,914 cases were reported in Chittagong city, 2,098 in different upazilas and 531 among patients who came from other districts.
Among the upazilas, Sitakunda recorded the highest number of cases at 620, followed by Karnaphuli with 285, Banshkhali 154, Rangunia 152, Satkania 121, Anwara 112, Raozan 103 and Patiya 100.
Other cases were reported in Hathazari (84), Chandanaish (77), Boalkhali (76), Mirsharai (79), Lohagara (66), Fatikchhari (44) and Sandwip (25).
Of the total dengue patients recorded this year, 2,402 are men, 1,403 are women and 1,109 are children.
Among the 107 patients admitted in the 24-hour period, 56 were men, 23 were women and 28 were children.
However, women accounted for the highest number of deaths. Of the 21 people who died, 11 were women, six were children and four were men.
The number of dengue cases recorded in Chittagong this year has already surpassed the totals for the previous two years.
The district recorded 4,323 cases and 45 deaths in 2024, while 4,864 cases and 27 deaths were reported in 2025.
As of October 5 this year, the number of cases stood at 4,914, with 21 deaths.
Residents have complained that mosquito-control activities in Chittagong have not kept pace with the rising number of dengue cases.
Muntasir Uddin, a resident of Sangeet Residential Area in Hamzarbag, said mosquito infestations in the area had become severe, while City Corporation workers assigned to mosquito control were rarely seen.
He also alleged a lack of supervision over the effectiveness of insecticide spraying.
Jamal Uddin, a resident of Chandanpura, said the number of dengue patients in the city had increased significantly, but City Corporation monitoring had not increased proportionately.
District Civil Surgeon Mohammad Sajedur Rahman told Bangla Tribune that dengue is a mosquito-borne disease and urged residents to keep their surroundings clean.
He said dengue could be controlled by destroying mosquito breeding grounds and advised people to undergo dengue tests and seek medical advice promptly if they develop a fever.
Sheikh Fazle Rabbi, divisional director of health in Chittagong, also advised people to consult a doctor immediately if they develop fever or symptoms of dengue.
He said the most important measure to prevent dengue was to destroy Aedes mosquito breeding grounds, while efforts should also be made to eliminate adult mosquitoes.
He said the City Corporation had been sent several letters urging it to intensify mosquito-control activities.
Ashraful Amin, chief executive officer and secretary of Chittagong City Corporation, told Bangla Tribune that the corporation was conducting regular mosquito-control activities to combat dengue and other mosquito-borne diseases.
He said special “crash programmes” were also being conducted in different areas when necessary.
Amin said dengue could not be controlled through insecticide spraying alone and stressed the need to destroy mosquito breeding grounds.
He also urged residents to prevent water from stagnating in and around their homes, rooftops, construction sites and other areas.

Dhaka ranks first globally in air pollution
item.description:
Dhaka ranked first among the world's most polluted cities on Tuesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 213 at 11:10am.
The air quality was classified as "very unhealthy", signalling a serious health alert where everyone may experience health effects, according to the AQI scale.
Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia ranked second with an AQI score of 208, while Singapore in Singapore ranked third with a score of 179 and Kolkata in India ranked fourth with an AQI score of 177.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while 151 to 200 is classified as "unhealthy". A reading between 201 and 300 is considered "very unhealthy", while levels above 301 are deemed "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

COP31 eyes modest steps as climate disasters multiply
item.description:
Nations reeling from a year of climate devastation gather for COP31 next month, but negotiations are not expected to deliver major progress in cutting the fossil fuels driving the crisis.
The conference follows deadly heatwaves and fires in Europe, catastrophic floods in Nepal and record temperatures around the world, testing whether the United Nations-backed talks can keep pace with reality.
As leaders meet in Turkey, an exceptionally powerful El Niño pattern will be approaching peak strength, threatening to amplify weather chaos worldwide and drive global heat to unprecedented highs.
Concerns over energy security will also loom large, with no end in sight to the Middle East war that has sent oil and gas prices soaring and hit fossil fuel-importing nations hard.
With a new agreement on fossil fuels unlikely, Turkey is rallying support for a voluntary "electrification" pledge it says could cut heat-trapping emissions and reduce reliance on energy imports.
"In many ways, the defining contexts for this year's climate summit will be heat and Hormuz," said David Waskow from the World Resources Institute, referencing the vital strait that carried one-fifth of the world's hydrocarbons before the Iran war.
Unusually, Turkey must navigate these complexities with Australia, a major fossil fuel exporter, after both countries agreed to share COP31 duties following a bruising hosting battle.
Australia's Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations in Antalya starting November 9, said this year's extreme events "show climate change is not a future challenge".
"It is a present reality... and the costs of inaction are rising," he said.
A "pre-COP" meeting began Monday in the climate-vulnerable Pacific with a leaders' retreat in Tuvalu and government meetings in Fiji.
Unlike recent COPs -- where nearly 200 nations forged landmark pacts on phasing down coal or moving away from fossil fuels -- the negotiation agenda at COP31 is light on big-ticket items.
There are more than 100 items on the table but many deal with technical matters, like approving indicators to track progress on climate adaptation.
"Much of the Antalya summit will be a 'roll up the sleeves' effort. Governments need to make concrete headway in negotiations, though there may not be dramatic outcomes this year," Waskow told AFP.
Nations are not expected to adopt new binding commitments to reduce the burning of fossil fuels -- the leading cause of climate change.
Countries agreed in 2023 to move away from coal, oil and gas but since then efforts to negotiate concrete targets or timelines for that transition have gone nowhere.
At last year's summit, fossil fuels were not mentioned by name in the final agreement after oil and gas-producing nations prevented consensus on the issue.
"Everyone agrees there will be no real gain at the multilateral level at the moment," Marta Torres-Gunfaus from the IDDRI think tank told AFP.
Fossil fuel emissions, meanwhile, hit record highs in 2025.
In September, the UN conceded that the milestone 1.5C climate target will be missed in a matter of years.
Nations frustrated at the COP gridlock have sought progress elsewhere.
Nearly 60 countries attended a fossil fuel phaseout conference without UN involvement this year.
France, the Netherlands and Germany have published "roadmaps" with explicit deadlines for quitting coal, oil and gas.
UN Climate chief Simon Stiell has defended the negotiations while acknowledging their limitations: "No single COP can fix this global crisis, but each takes meaningful steps forward," he said.
Turkey says it is not realistic to expect all countries to move at the same pace.
"Any proposal that fails to reconcile our climate objectives with social and economic realities will be doomed to fail," said Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Turkey is curating an "action agenda" alongside the negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.
There is broad support for its centrepiece goal: raising the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20% on Tuesday to 35% by 2035.
The electrification target does not state how that extra power should be produced. One-third of electricity is generated by coal, and there are concerns the target could provide cover for expanded fossil fuel use.
The Nepal floods would also put "a huge amount of pressure" on western countries to increase financial support for climate disaster recovery, said Ajay Mathur, a former Indian government negotiator.
"We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying for it," Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said.

Tangail eyes tourism boom with rich heritage and natural beauty
item.description:
Rich in history, cultural heritage, and natural beauty, Tangail has vast potential to develop as a major tourism destination, with its historic landmarks, forests, traditional handloom industry, and distinctive products offering a diverse experience for visitors.
The district is home to Mughal-era Atia Mosque, Mohera, Hemnagar, Karotia, Delduar, Pakutia, and Dhanbari zamindar mansions, Madhupur National Park, Pirgachha Rubber Garden, and Jamuna Bridge. Its proximity to Dhaka and relatively easy road connectivity further enhance its prospects as a tourism hub.
Tourism could also generate employment for local guides, resort operators, restaurants, and handicraft businesses while creating opportunities for increased local revenue through public-private investment.
Among the district's natural attractions, Madhupur National Park stands out for its extensive forest landscape and wildlife. Spread across more than 20,000 acres, the park offers visitors a break from urban life. It is also home to a deer breeding centre.
Pirgachha Rubber Garden in Madhupur is another popular destination. Visitors can enjoy the changing appearance of its large rubber trees across the seasons and, with permission, observe the process of collecting and processing raw rubber at a nearby factory.
Atia Mosque in Delduar is one of Tangail's notable historical landmarks. Built in a distinctive Mughal-Sultanate architectural style, the single-domed mosque was once featured on the Tk10 banknote. The 201-domed mosque in Gopalpur is another attraction, featuring eight tall minarets, four of which are 101 feet high.
The Jamuna Bridge area in Kalihati draws visitors for its river views, open air, and sunrise and sunset scenes. The nearby Jamuna Railway Bridge has also become an attraction.
Upendra Sarobar in Nagarpur, around 25km from Tangail town, is another scenic destination. The lake, locally known as “Baro Ghatla Dighi,” has 12 ghats and was excavated in 1341 Bengali calendar to address the area's drinking water shortage.
Tangail's cultural identity is further strengthened by Porabari Chamcham, a traditional sweet with a history of around two centuries, and its famous handloom sarees. Visitors can explore the district's historic zamindar mansions, particularly Mohera Zamindar Bari, one of the most popular heritage sites.
Local residents say the tourism sector needs better preservation of historical sites, quality hotels, and resorts, improved security, and stronger digital promotion to reach domestic and international tourists.
Tangail Deputy Commissioner Sharifa Haque said the district's 12 upazilas offered diverse natural and cultural attractions. “Tourism can play an important role in the local economy. We have to present Tangail's history, heritage, culture, and natural beauty to the world, and we are working towards that goal,” she said.
Local lawmaker and State Minister Sultan Salahuddin Tuku said plans were underway to develop Tangail as a modern tourism hub, including a mini tourism centre around the DC Lake and a larger tourism destination in the char areas.
He said improved connectivity, cleanliness, scenic development, and tourist facilities would be essential to unlock the district's tourism potential and create more employment opportunities.

item.title: Case filed over attack on journalists at RU
item.description:
A case was filed against unidentified people on Monday over an attack on journalists on the Rajshahi University (RU) campus allegedly by leaders and activists of Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD).
Md Munir Hossain, deputy registrar of Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Hall, filed the case with Motihar Police Station, said its Officer-in-Charge Golam Kabir.
“We have recorded a case. We have started working on it and will take action after investigation,” he said.
However, journalists covering the university expressed dissatisfaction over the decision to file the case against unidentified suspects.
They demanded that those involved in the attack be identified and arrested quickly and that the university administration take visible and effective action against them.
Ashiqul Islam Dhrubo, president of RU Press Club, said there was no ambiguity about the identities of those involved in the attack.
“We have all the footage of the attack, and people across the country have seen it. It is as clear as daylight who was involved. Their names, posts and identities have already been published in news reports,” he said.
“There is no question of filing a case against unidentified persons. We demand that the names of everyone involved be included in the case and that they be arrested as soon as possible,” Ashiqul added.
Former RU Journalists’ Association President Irfan Tamim also criticised the decision, describing it as extremely disappointing.
Ten people, including four journalists, were injured when JCD leaders and activists allegedly attacked them in front of Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Hall around 8:30pm on Sunday.
Several JCD leaders and activists, including university unit Vice-President Ahsan Habib, were alleged to have been involved in the attack.
The attack reportedly took place after journalists took photographs of locally made weapons allegedly displayed for an attack on a rival group.
The injured journalists include Arifuzzaman Qurban, RU correspondent of bdnews24.com; Zahidul Islam, correspondent of Agamir Somoy; Noor Ahsan Mridul, correspondent of The Daily Star; and Mainul Islam Raju, correspondent of Samakal.
Meanwhile, a five-member committee was formed to investigate the incident.

item.title: Remittance inflows up over 15% in current FY27
item.description:
Bangladesh has received $8.798 billion in remittances so far in FY27, sent to the country between July 1 and October 3.
This represents a 15.1% increase compared to the $7.643 billion received during the same period of the previous fiscal year.
Executive spokesperson of Bangladesh Bank Arief Hossain Khan confirmed the data on Sunday (October 4).
He noted that the significant growth in remittances was driven by an increase in funds sent home by Bangladeshi expatriate workers during the first few months of the current fiscal year.
According to Bangladesh Bank data, the country’s gross foreign exchange reserves stood at approximately $36.14 billion as of September 29.
Earlier on September 20, total foreign exchange reserves were at $36.30 billion.
According to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) BPM6 calculation method at that time, the reserve amount was $31.45 billion.
According to the central bank's updated report, remittances worth $1.877 billion arrived in the country during the first 20 days of September.
Of this, expatriates sent $130 million in just three days—from September 17 to 19—compared to $1.869 billion received in the first 19 days of September last year.

item.title: Experts: Bangladesh poultry must shift from volume to value
item.description:
Speakers at the International Technical Seminar 2026 organized by the World's Poultry Science Association – Bangladesh Branch (WPSA-BB) emphasized that Bangladesh's poultry sector must move beyond a volume-centric mindset and focus on farm profitability, food safety, climate resilience, and internationally credible standards.
Held under the theme "Resilient Poultry Production for Global Competitiveness", the seminar featured eight speakers representing the government, industry, and academia.
Md Shahzaman Khan, director general, Department of Livestock Services (DLS), attended the inaugural session as chief guest.
Special guests included Moshiur Rahman, convener, Bangladesh Poultry Industries Central Council (BPICC), and Shakila Faruque, director general, Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute (BLRI).
The session was chaired by WPSA-BB president Shamsul Arefin Khaled.
WPSA-BB president Shamsul Arefin Khaled stated that while the sector has addressed volume growth, it has yet to secure value realization.
Despite rising output, many producers are incurring losses; according to his estimates, breeder farms lost approximately Tk1,706 crore over the past 20 months.
He highlighted that profit margins have shifted from farms and hatcheries to intermediaries along the supply chain.
He urged aligning chick supply with market demand, according legal status to the national poultry policy, and expanding investments in insurance, processing, and cold chains.
Ensuring farmer protection and building a sustainable industry: WPSA-BB general secretary Fayzur Rahman outlined the strategic direction for the industry.
Md Zahidul Islam, director & CEO of Bangla-UK Agro Products Ltd, noted that the lowest FCR does not always yield the highest profitability. Adhering strictly to drug withdrawal periods and marketing heavier birds can improve farm income as well as food safety.
Khitima Jindamongkon, regional manager at dsm-firmenich APAC, shared insights from Asian poultry industries, noting that future success depends on integration, processing, traceability, and leveraging local breeds like the 'Sonali' chicken.
Prof Emdadul Haque Chowdhury, Department of Pathology at Bangladesh Agricultural University (BAU), presented a research study combining consumer/stakeholder surveys with laboratory testing. Contrary to public misconceptions, no growth hormones were detected in the tested samples.
Moshiur Rahman, managing director of Paragon Group and convener of BPICC, stated that optimizing feed conversion, efficient energy management, and reducing mortality can lower both operational costs and carbon emissions.
Baby Rani Karmakar, joint secretary at the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock, noted that while Bangladesh can compete in international halal markets, success requires internationally recognized certification, accredited laboratories, and market-specific compliance frameworks.
The seminar concluded with an open discussion titled "Towards a Globally Competitive, Safe, and Sustainable Poultry Sector in Bangladesh", moderated by Prof Md Mahmudul Hasan Sikder, member-secretary of the WPSA-BB technical sub-committee.
Discussions also focused on developing affordable, smart, resource-efficient farming models across scales and charting the strategic roadmap for the sector.

Plan International: Climate shocks disrupt girls’ education, health, safety
item.description:
Climate-related disasters are increasing the risks of child marriage, unintended pregnancy and violence among girls while disrupting their access to education and essential health services, a new global study by Plan International has found.
The report, "State of the World’s Girls 2026: Change Her Forecast", draws on research involving more than 5,000 girls and young women aged 15 to 24 in Bangladesh, Kenya, Peru, Senegal and Zimbabwe, alongside an analysis of climate and health data from 52 low- and middle-income countries spanning three decades.
The findings show that climate shocks such as floods, droughts, cyclones and extreme heat are putting additional pressure on families and communities and disrupting the systems girls depend on for their health, safety and education.
Nine in 10 girls surveyed said climate-related events were placing serious pressure on their families’ survival, health and stability.
Meanwhile, 76% said girls and young women in their communities were struggling to access at least one sexual or reproductive health service following climate-related events.
The study found that 36% of girls had seen more girls marry or enter unions before the age of 18 in their communities following climate-related disasters, while 33% reported seeing an increase in unintended pregnancies.
Another 28% observed an increase in violence against women and girls following climate-related events.
The disruption extends to menstrual health. Half of the girls surveyed said girls and young women in their communities were struggling to access menstrual products or clean water needed to manage menstruation.
The report also highlights how climate shocks can make sexual and reproductive healthcare harder to reach, including contraception, maternity care, menstrual health support, counselling and other essential services.
In Bangladesh, 19-year-old Shahina, who participated in the research, described how climate-related economic hardship can contribute to early marriage.
She said: “When floods leave people completely destitute, families think about financial hardship and marry off girls at a very young age.”
According to the report, girls also face increased risks of sexual exploitation after climate-related disasters when protection systems and support networks break down. Some girls reported being pressured to exchange sex for money or basic necessities.
Emergency shelters can also become unsafe, with girls reporting harassment and sexual violence in overcrowded and poorly lit conditions.
The research identifies education as one of the strongest protective factors for girls during climate crises.
Girls whose education is disrupted are twice as likely to marry young or experience an unintended pregnancy, according to the report.
Schools provide girls with education as well as access to information about their rights, health and available services, while also providing support networks that can help protect them from exploitation and early marriage.
The report also highlights the particular risks associated with prolonged drought.
An analysis covering 52 countries over three decades found prolonged drought to be the climate hazard most consistently associated with increasing rates of child marriage and early unions.
As drought destroys crops, livestock and household income over time, families facing financial hardship may resort to marrying off their daughters, the report said.
Reena Ghelani, chief executive officer of Plan International, said: “Girls cannot continue to be treated as an afterthought in climate action. They must have a meaningful say in the decisions that shape their lives, and their rights and needs must be built into climate policy and financing from the outset.”
Ghelani also said climate change was already affecting girls’ education and access to health services.
She added: “Only half of national climate plans mention girls’ or women’s health, and despite the escalating impact of climate shocks on the health systems and services girls rely on, just 0.5% of multilateral climate finance supports health.”
The report calls on governments and donors to keep schools open and free during climate shocks and allocate a defined share of climate adaptation finance to adolescent girls’ health, including sexual and reproductive health services, contraception and maternity care.
It also recommends that menstrual products, contraception and protection services be included in emergency response packages from the beginning rather than being treated as later interventions.
Plan International further called for targeted support for girls from minority communities, girls with disabilities and those already displaced, who face greater barriers to accessing essential services.
The organisation urged governments and donors to put girls at the centre of climate policy, financing and disaster response, arguing that their experiences and leadership should help shape decisions affecting their lives.
The report comes ahead of COP31, where countries are expected to negotiate further international action on climate change.

item.title: Attack on New Gini Properties: Maj Gen (retd) Mohiuddin gets bail
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Monday granted bail to Major General (retd) Golam Mohiuddin Chowdhury in a case filed over the attack, vandalism and looting at a New Gini Properties housing project, including at content creator Salman Mohammad Muqtadir's "Brownfish Studio", in the South Manikdi area of the capital.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid passed the order after hearing a bail petition filed by the defense.
The court granted him bail on a Tk 2,000 bond until the next scheduled date, according to his lawyers.
The next date for submitting the investigation report in the case has been set for October 28.
Golam Mohiuddin was arrested by the Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police from a house in the capital's Segunbagicha area on September 30.
New Gini Properties Director Saiful Islam Bhuiyan filed the case with Cantonment Police Station over the attack on the housing project near the ECB Chattar on the night of September 26.
Salman Muqtadir's "Brownfish Studio", located inside the housing project, was also attacked, vandalized and looted.
According to the case statement, a group of people, equipped with weapons, entered the project area and opened fire before attacking with machetes, knives and sticks. At one stage, they entered Salman Muqtadir's studio and vandalized and looted it.
The complaint alleged that cash, laptops, computers, cameras, professional media equipment and other valuables were looted, while vehicles were also vandalized.
Several people, including site engineer Md Parvez, were injured in the attack.
The complainant alleged that the incident caused losses of around Tk 1.42 crore to the company and that goods worth Tk 1.50 crore were allegedly stolen.
Thirteen people were named in the case, while another 150 to 200 unidentified people were accused.

item.title: Lightning strike leaves 18 students ill at Gazipur school
item.description:
At least 18 students fell ill after lightning struck near Singua Bahumukhi High School in Kapasia upazila of Gazipur on Monday afternoon.
The affected students were taken to Monohardi Upazila Health Complex in neighbouring Narsingdi for treatment. The incident occurred around noon while classes were underway at the school.
Local residents said heavy rain began in the afternoon, followed by several lightning strikes. Hearing students crying from the school’s ground floor, residents rushed to the building and found several students lying on the floor and benches in an almost unconscious state.
Headteacher Mostafizur Rahman said several consecutive lightning strikes occurred around 2:00pm, leaving at least 18 female students on the ground floor sick.
Teachers and local residents took the affected students to Monohardi Upazila Health Complex. Six were admitted for treatment, while the others were sent home after receiving first aid.
A Matin, a senior staff nurse at the health complex, said six students had been admitted and were receiving treatment. The others were discharged after receiving primary treatment.

item.title: PM Tarique joins World Habitat Day discussion
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday joined a discussion marking World Habitat Day 2026, focusing on universal housing and sustainable urbanisation.
The program, organised by the Ministry of Housing and Public Works, is being held at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre in Dhaka under the theme “Universal Housing, Sustainable Urbanisation.”
Before joining the program, the prime minister planted a Swarna Champa on the premises of the conference centre.
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo, Housing and Public Works Minister Zakaria Taher Sumon, State Minister for Housing and Public Works Ahmad Sohel Manzur and ministry secretary Md Obaidur Rahman, among others, joined the programme.
A three-day housing fair has been organised at the lobby of the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre as part of the World Habitat Day observance.
A total of 157 stalls have been set up at the fair, featuring housing and construction sector products and services, banking services, Rajuk, the Department of Architecture, the Public Works Department and other agencies under the Ministry of Housing and Public Works.
The prime minister is expected to inaugurate the fair after the discussion program.
A seminar on planned urbanisation and sustainable housing will also be held at the conference centre at 2:30pm.
World Habitat Day is also being observed across all divisions and districts of the country through various programs, including publication of a souvenir, special discussions on television and radio, and displaying banners, posters and festoons at important locations.
Since 1986, World Habitat Day has been observed in Bangladesh and countries around the world.

item.title: Indian police accused of sexually harassing journalists at protest
item.description:
Three female journalists have accused Delhi Police personnel of sexual harassment while covering protests in the Indian capital against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, reports BBC.
The allegations were made on Saturday after police detained scores of protesters demanding Kumar’s resignation.
Delhi Police said the New Delhi district had received the complaints and transferred them to the Crime Branch for a “fair and impartial” inquiry.
Thousands of protesters gathered in Delhi and Mumbai on Sunday for a third consecutive day, demanding Kumar’s resignation over changes to voter rolls. The Election Commission says the revision aims to remove duplicate and ineligible entries, while opposition parties and protesters allege the process could disenfranchise eligible voters and benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The BJP and Election Commission have rejected the allegations.
Videos circulating online showed protesters being detained and dragged away from the Jantar Mantar protest site in central Delhi.
The journalists’ allegations include inappropriate touching by police personnel. One journalist has also accused an assistant commissioner of police of sexually assaulting her while she was recording police action. The complaints are being investigated by the Crime Branch.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said women fear for their safety and that the Home Ministry must answer for the incident.
“Police dragged me by my hair,” Aahna Singh, an activist and student at Jawaharlal Nehru University, told Reuters during the protests. She accused police of “brutality.”
The Press Club of India has condemned the alleged treatment of journalists during the protests and demanded immediate action on the complaints against police personnel.
The organisation said it was “shocked and dismayed” by the reported treatment of journalists, adding that journalists must be allowed to work freely and document protests without fear.
The protesters say the voter-roll revision will benefit the BJP.
The Election Commission, however, says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries and update voter rolls to account for people who have died, left the country or registered at more than one address.
The revision, known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), has been controversial, with opposition parties accusing the Election Commission of manipulating voter rolls to favour the BJP. The BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the allegations.
The protests have included supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as an online satirical movement and has since become a youth-led political pressure group.
The CJP called for the latest protests following reports that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections to decisions and orders issued by Kumar.
The Election Commission has defended its decision-making process, saying differing views are part of the process and that decisions were taken unanimously.
The reported differences have further fuelled opposition demands for Kumar’s resignation.

Unplanned urbanization puts Dhaka at growing risk
item.description:
Dhaka is becoming increasingly difficult to live in as unplanned urbanization, rising population density, and inadequate civic infrastructure continue to put pressure on the capital.
The city lacks sufficient roads, open spaces, green areas, playgrounds and water bodies, while access to affordable housing remains a major challenge for low- and lower-middle-income households.
Urban planners warn that unless population density, building intensity and development are brought under effective control, Dhaka's liveability will continue to deteriorate.
The concerns come as Bangladesh observes World Habitat Day on Monday under the theme “Universal Housing, Sustainable Urbanization.”
The day is observed globally on the first Monday of October every year following a decision by the UN General Assembly in 1985. It has been observed since 1986 to raise awareness about housing, human settlements and sustainable urban development.
In Bangladesh, the Ministry of Housing and Public Works has arranged a discussion at the National Osmani Memorial Auditorium at 10am today to mark the occasion.
But experts say the reality of Dhaka's urban development remains far removed from the goal of sustainable and inclusive housing.
According to the Population and Housing Census 2022, Dhaka division has the country's highest population density, with 2,156 people living per square kilometre.
The enormous concentration of people in the capital and its surrounding areas has placed growing pressure on housing, roads, drainage, water supply, sanitation, waste management and other essential services.
Urban planners say simply constructing more high-rise buildings cannot solve Dhaka's housing crisis.
Housing must be planned alongside schools, hospitals, community centres, roads, parks, playgrounds, water bodies and other civic facilities, they say.
Adequate natural light and ventilation, green spaces and open areas must also be ensured within residential developments.
Instead, the rapid expansion of buildings and the drive to maximise land use have often taken precedence over broader urban planning considerations.
The housing crisis is particularly severe for low- and lower-middle-income residents.
While the private sector continues to develop high-end apartments and housing projects, affordable housing options for low-income households remain inadequate.
In this regard, Professor Dr Adil Muhammad Khan, executive director of the Institute for Planning and Development (IPD), said the constitutional commitment to ensure adequate housing has not translated into equal access to housing opportunities.
“Disparities in housing are increasing day by day,” he said.
According to him, government investment in housing and settlements for low- and lower-middle-income people in urban areas remains inadequate.
“Sustainable cities and human settlements cannot be built by leaving the housing sector solely to the profit-driven approach and strategies of the private sector,” he said.
He called for large-scale affordable housing projects for low-income groups, alongside measures to control Dhaka's population growth, manage density and strengthen development controls.
The Dhaka Detailed Area Plan (DAP), prepared to guide the capital's future development, was approved in August 2022.
The plan sought to control building intensity, housing density and the number of flats that could be constructed in different areas, with the broader objective of making Dhaka more liveable.
However, landowners and real estate developers strongly opposed several provisions of the plan.
Some amendments were introduced in September 2023 following their demands. But the changes failed to satisfy all stakeholders, prompting another initiative to revise the DAP.
Following the political change in 2024, the interim government formed a high-level advisory committee on the issue.
Based on recommendations from the committee, the DAP was revised for a second time, with a gazette notification issued in December 2025.
Urban planners have strongly criticised the repeated revisions, arguing that a long-term metropolitan development plan should not be repeatedly altered before its effectiveness can even be properly assessed.
Professor Adil said the success or failure of any urban plan ultimately depends on political commitment, proper enforcement, adequate financing, development control, the rule of law and impartial implementation in the public interest.
He said the 2022 DAP contained specific proposals addressing many of these issues.
“Yet within three years of its approval, the plan was amended twice under pressure from real estate interests, increasing floor area ratios (FAR), housing units and population density in various areas,” he said.
At the same time, he said, proposals for affordable housing, neighbourhood parks, playgrounds, primary schools and other civic facilities have remained largely unimplemented.
He argued that Dhaka's declining liveability was not caused by a lack of plans.
Rather, the failure to properly implement previous structure plans, master plans and DAPs has been a major reason behind the city's worsening conditions.
Professor Adil said the issue of population-density zoning had been compromised from the beginning.
According to him, the authorities gradually moved away from area-based height zoning proposed in the draft DAP towards an FAR-based approach, followed by increases in permissible FAR in different areas.
“This was a compromise at every stage,” he said.
He stressed that a liveable city requires not only population-density planning but also effective management of development intensity.
He also warned that amendments allowing greater construction intensity could restrict the flow of natural light and air into buildings, potentially creating further public health risks.
The concern is particularly important in a densely populated megacity where ventilation, open space and access to greenery are already limited.
The Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha (Rajuk), however, maintains that the DAP remains essential for planned housing and urban development.
Ashraful Islam, chief urban planner of Rajuk and project director of the DAP, said the plan was prepared to transform Dhaka into a functional and liveable metropolitan city.
He said 58 areas have been identified under the DAP for affordable housing targeting low- and lower-middle-income households.
Under the proposed arrangements, low-income residents would have opportunities to own homes through affordable housing schemes and long-term instalment payments.
The revised DAP has been sent to the Planning Commission for approval, he said, adding that implementation would begin after approval.
Urban experts say Dhaka's fundamental problem is not a shortage of plans but weak implementation and inadequate development control.
Over the years, successive plans have been prepared to address congestion, housing, transport and environmental challenges. Yet implementation has frequently fallen behind the pace of urban expansion.
The result is a city where population and building density are rising while roads, parks, playgrounds, water bodies and other public amenities continue to shrink.
Experts argue that repeatedly changing planning regulations without ensuring basic civic infrastructure risks further worsening the imbalance between private development and public interest.
For Dhaka to remain liveable, they say, authorities must prioritise affordable housing, control population density, protect open spaces and water bodies, expand green areas and ensure schools, hospitals, roads and other essential services alongside residential development.
The challenge is therefore no longer simply to prepare another plan for Dhaka.

item.title: ACC case: Shajahan Khan, son shown arrested
item.description:
The Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) has filed a case against former shipping minister Shajahan Khan and his son, Ashibur Rahman Khan, over allegations of acquiring and possessing assets worth Tk9.89 crore disproportionate to their known sources of income.
A Dhaka court on Monday ordered that the two be shown arrested in the case.
Dhaka Metropolitan Senior Special Judge Shahjahan Kabir passed the order following an application filed on September 7 by ACC Assistant Director Mahathir Muhammad Samir, who is investigating the case.
ACC lawyer Mohammad Khadimul Haque confirmed the matter.
While being taken from the court, Shajahan Khan told journalists: “You will see who speaks their mind.”
He also commented on the National Citizens Party (NCP) and Jamaat-e-Islami, saying: “By aligning with Jamaat-e-Islami, the NCP has effectively become Jamaat-e-Islami.”
During the hearing, defence lawyer Mizanur Rahman Badsha opposed the application to show the accused arrested.
He argued that the allegations and the filing of the case did not follow proper procedures.
The lawyer said nine bank accounts were mentioned in the case, three of which were in Shajahan Khan’s name, while the others were joint accounts. He also claimed that the value of the assets had been inflated in the allegations.
He said Ashib had paid taxes on the assets in accordance with the law.
The defence also sought bail, with the court fixing October 15 for a hearing on the petition.
According to the ACC case statement, movable and immovable assets worth Tk11.79 crore were found in Ashibur Rahman’s name.
The investigation found that his legitimate sources of income amounted to Tk1.90 crore.
The ACC said it found evidence of assets worth Tk9.89 crore that were disproportionate to his known sources of income.
The investigation report further alleged that Shajahan Khan, while serving as a member of parliament and minister, abused his position to facilitate the acquisition of the assets in his son’s name using funds obtained through dishonest means, both directly and indirectly.
ACC Deputy Director Kamlesh Mondal filed the case as the complainant on February 2, 2025.
The court has set November 25 for submission of the investigation report.

item.title: Appeal filed seeking to increase Inu's sentence for crimes against humanity
item.description:
An appeal has been filed seeking an increase in the sentence handed down to Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal (Jasad) President Hasanul Haq Inu by the International Crimes Tribunal in a case involving crimes against humanity, including the killing of six people in Kushtia during the July-August mass uprising.
Prosecutor Gazi MH Tamim confirmed the matter on Monday.
On June 30, the International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Inu to 10 years in prison and fined him Tk1 lakh.
The verdict was delivered by a tribunal bench led by Justice Nazrul Islam Chowdhury, chairman of International Crimes Tribunal-2.
Eight charges were brought against Inu. The tribunal sentenced him to 10 years in prison on the third charge. For charges 6 and 7, he was sentenced to 10 years in prison on each count and ordered to pay Tk1 lakh in compensation for each, totalling Tk2 lakh.
However, the tribunal acquitted him of charges 1, 2, 4, 5 and 8.
Despite the separate sentences, the tribunal ordered that the sentences be served concurrently, meaning Inu will serve a total of 10 years in prison.
On May 14, after hearing arguments from both sides, the tribunal kept the case under Curia Advisari Vult (CAV), meaning the verdict was reserved for a later date.
Prosecutors Faruk Ahammad, Moinul Karim and Abdus Sobhan Tarafder, among others, represented the prosecution at the hearing. Senior lawyer Mansurul Haque Chowdhury represented Inu and concluded the defence arguments.
The defence presented its arguments over nine days, highlighting various legal issues in Inu's favour. It also argued that Inu was not a member of parliament during the July 2024 mass uprising.
Mansurul Haque said Inu had no involvement in the killing of the six people in Kushtia. Witnesses in the case also said he was not present in Kushtia when the killings took place.
The verdict was subsequently published on September 20 after being signed by the tribunal bench led by Justice Nazrul Islam Chowdhury.
On August 5, 2024, amid the July-August movement, gunfire was reported at several locations in Kushtia town, killing six people: worker Ashraful Islam, Suruj Ali Babu, students Abdullah Al Mustakin and Usama, businessman Bablu Faraji, and employee Yusuf Sheikh.
Several others were also injured in the violence.
A case was later filed against Inu at the International Crimes Tribunal in connection with the killings. Based on an investigation agency report, the prosecution subsequently submitted formal charges outlining eight allegations against him.

item.title: Heightened security planned at 781 Durga Puja mandaps in Faridpur
item.description:
Extensive security measures have been taken at 781 puja mandaps in Faridpur ahead of Durga Puja, the biggest religious festival of the Hindu community.
The authorities have directed the organisers to install CCTV cameras, ensure adequate lighting and deploy volunteers at each venue.
The directives were issued at a meeting held at the conference room of the Faridpur deputy commissioner on Sunday with Deputy Commissioner Mazharul Islam in the chair.
Members of Puja Udjapon Committees, senior officials of government agencies and civil society representatives were present at the meeting and discussed the issues of security, law and order, traffic management and idol immersion arrangements at the puja venues.
The puja mandaps will be categorised based on security risks, with security arrangements strengthened accordingly.
Police, Ansar and Village Defence Party (VDP) members will be deployed at the puja venues while plainclothes police and intelligence personnel will also remain on duty.
Shahriar Mohammad Miaji, Superintendent of Faridpur Police, said the district police have made all-out preparations to ensure that Durga Puja is celebrated in a safe and peaceful environment while maintaining communal harmony and mutual goodwill.
Deputy Commissioner Mazharul Islam said the administration has taken all necessary measures to ensure peaceful and uninterrupted celebrations. He urged people to maintain tolerance, harmony and goodwill during the festival.
The authorities also instructed the organisers to strictly follow the designated schedules and routes for idol immersion. They advised against playing drums or other musical instruments at high volume during Maghrib and Isha prayer times in order to maintain religious harmony.
The district police’s cybercrime monitoring cell will remain active round the clock to prevent attempts to disrupt communal harmony through rumours, misleading information or provocative posts on social media.
People have been advised to contact the national emergency service 999 or the Faridpur Police Control Room in case of any emergency.

item.title: 12kg LPG cylinder price rises to Tk 1,837
item.description:
The Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) has raised the price of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), setting the price of a 12kg cylinder at Tk 1,837, up from Tk 1,585.
The new price, an increase of Tk 252, will take effect from 6:00pm on Sunday.
The regulator has also raised the price of autogas, used in vehicles, to Tk 84.62 per litre from Tk 73.09.
The price hike comes amid a severe LPG shortage in the market and allegations that cylinders were being sold at inflated prices. Some had claimed the shortage was artificial, while others argued that a price increase would help restore normal supplies.
BERC said the latest adjustment was made in response to higher international LPG prices, shipping costs and diesel prices used for transportation.
Consumers had reported difficulties finding LPG cylinders in the two weeks before the new price was announced, although traders denied any shortage.
In September, there were also allegations that 12kg cylinders, officially priced at Tk 1,585, were being sold for Tk 2,200 to Tk 2,500.
It remains to be seen whether LPG supplies will return to normal following the price hike.

item.title: Baridhara crash: Court rejects teen’s bail plea
item.description:
A Dhaka court has rejected the bail petition of the 17-year-old boy accused in the death of construction worker Mehedi Hasan Mim in a car crash in Baridhara, with the judge saying his continued detention could send a “positive message” to children.
Dhaka Juvenile Court-8 Judge Md Abdul Moktadir passed the order on Sunday after hearing the bail petition.
“The boy’s release at the earliest stage would send a negative message to society. But keeping him detained could send a positive message to children,” the judge said.
State counsel Mohammad Sharif Uddin Mamun confirmed the bail rejection.
The case concerns the death of 24-year-old Mehedi, who was sitting on a footpath on Road 1 in Baridhara Diplomatic Zone around 5pm on September 22 when a speeding private car lost control and ran him over. He was taken to Kurmitola General Hospital, where doctors declared him dead.
People at the scene detained a teenager who was in the driver’s seat and handed him over to police. Police released him into his uncle’s custody later that night after questioning.
Mehedi’s brother Moktadir Islam filed a case with Gulshan police on September 23, naming Akash Mark as the accused driver but not naming the teenager.
Following criticism over his release, police took the teenager into custody the same day and produced him before court on September 24, seeking his detention at the Child Development Centre in Gazipur.
The teenager’s lawyers later sought bail, saying the victim’s family had reached a Tk9 lakh settlement.
During Sunday’s hearing, defence lawyer Md Golam Mostofa Khan argued that the teenager was not driving the car and had only been inside it. He also cited the settlement between the families.
The state opposed bail, saying the case was serious and that the teenager was involved in the incident while the car was being driven recklessly. The prosecution also said he did not have a driving licence.
The judge referred to CCTV footage that allegedly showed the teenager getting out from the driver’s side and said police had found preliminary evidence of his involvement.
The judge also said releasing him could create the impression that someone could drive recklessly, cause an accident and still secure bail quickly.
The court subsequently rejected the bail petition.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,125 as three die in 24 hours
item.description:
Three more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Sunday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,125.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all three of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,023, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 102, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the three new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in Dhaka, with two deaths reported in both the Dhaka division and Dhaka district.
A total of 1,218 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Sunday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 196,418.
During the same period, 82 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 21,748.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 174,149 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 166,908 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Dengue: Six more die, 2,089 hospitalized in 24 hours
item.description:

"Out of 2,089, 203 patients were hospitalized in Barisal division, 324 in Chittagong division, 514 in Dhaka division, 196 in Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) and 106 in Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) areas, 330 in Khulna division, 99 in Mymensingh division, 224 in Rajshahi division, 83 in Rangpur division and 10 Sylhet division, a Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) statement said.
Since the start of the dengue onslaughts, Bangladesh this year witnessed so far 262 deaths while the disease inflicted 86,458.
The dengue last year claimed 413 lives and inflicted 1,02,861 people in the country.
Besides, the dengue claimed 575 lives and inflicted 1,01,214 people in 2024.

item.title: ICT sets Oct 6 to complete testimony in Ziaul Ahsan case
item.description:
The International Crimes Tribunal has set October 6 to complete the testimony of the investigation officer in the crimes against humanity case against Major General (retd) Ziaul Ahsan over allegations of enforced disappearance and killing of more than 100 people during the Awami League government.
Tribunal-1 passed the order on Sunday following a prosecution petition. Earlier, investigation officer Md Rafiqul Islam gave partial testimony on September 30.
The prosecution said three charges had been brought against Ziaul Ahsan following a lengthy investigation. A formal charge was filed against him on December 17, 2025, and the tribunal framed charges and ordered the trial to begin on January 14, 2026.
Ziaul Ahsan served as director general of the National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC). He was arrested in mid-August 2024.
The prosecution said the state’s presentation of evidence would conclude with the completion of the investigation officer’s testimony. The defence will then have an opportunity to present its evidence, followed by the arguments stage.
Prosecutor Gazi MH Tamim had earlier said the prosecution believed it had established the charges against Ziaul Ahsan through the testimony of 15 witnesses.

item.title: Mahfuz Anam: Groups that dismantle autocracy become each other’s enemies
item.description:
The Daily Star Editor and Publisher Mahfuz Anam said groups that unite to dismantle an autocratic system eventually become each other’s enemies, causing repeated failures to institutionalize democracy in Bangladesh.
He made the remarks on Sunday, on the second day of the three-day Bay of Bengal Conversation 2026, organized by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS), at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka.
Mahfuz Anam said: “In the past, instead of institutionalizing free and fair elections, we increasingly fell into conflict, competition and then destruction, and I think we failed because we really do not know how to run our country. We actually do not know what governance is. We really do not know how to bring together a people with all their strength, all their innovation, all their resilience and turn that source into national development.”
“In my view, one reason is that the nation becomes united while dismantling a dictatorship, but once the dictatorship is dismantled, the nation becomes divided. The groups that work together to destroy the dictatorship become each other’s enemies, and that is where we have repeatedly, repeatedly and repeatedly failed to institutionalize the rebuilding of democracy in Bangladesh.”
Mahfuz Anam said Bangladesh had an almost endless capacity to fail to build democracy after dismantling autocratic systems.
“Unfortunately, we have an almost endless capacity that we cannot build democracy after dismantling autocracy. We were born again as Bangladesh, which was against a very brutal military dictatorship, but we failed to build a democratic Bangladesh and then there was a military coup. Ershad fell and we returned to democracy in 1991, and we really hoped that this would be the rebirth of democracy in Bangladesh, and we had several elections under a caretaker government.”
“However, and in my view the reason is that in Bangladesh we have over-politicized every institution imaginable.”
He said: “Doctors are divided over which political party you belong to. They are divided in many other professions, including journalism. You have pro-BNP journalists, you have pro-Jamaat journalists. I mean, how can a journalist be pro-politics? I mean, you can have a personal preference and of course you are free to vote, but in a profession where credibility is your life responsibility, how can you publicly support a political party and still expect to enjoy credibility?”
Mahfuz Anam said excessive politicization had eroded the functioning of almost all institutions.
“So we have a system where excessive politicization in one way has eroded the functioning of almost all our institutions. You really run a country through an efficient bureaucracy. We have been politicized. The police are always used as a partisan extension of your party. Muscle power and intelligence agencies are again used for political purposes.”
“So constitutional bodies such as the Anti-Corruption Commission and the Information Commission, these bodies which are considered constitutional bodies and are independently operated, are all politicized. So, to cut a long story short, the truth is that we are so good at destroying autocracy, but the sad reality is that we are so bad at building democratic institutions.”
Mahfuz Anam said the main problem was excessive politicization, which had caused the entire governance system to fail.
“So when a party is elected through the democratic process, we celebrate the expression of the people’s will. But very soon we realize that the outcome of that election result is transformed into political reality instead of public interest.”
“Obviously, it is worldwide that every political party, whether the Labor Party wins in England, or the Democrats or Republicans win in the United States, there will be some partisanship. But turning your entire governance system into an extension of your own party is where the decline begins, and one of the first consequences is corruption.”
“One of its first consequences is nepotism and partisan favoritism. Day after day, month after month and year after year, our entire governance system collapses.”
He said modern technology had made governance a science.
“Now with modern technology, governance is a science. Governance is not just good wishes and dreaming a dream. Governance is how you translate that dream. Technology can now give us a highly efficient bureaucracy and an efficient police force and, at the same time, a fair police force.”
“And here I think Bangladesh now faces its biggest challenge, if we want to move forward. Because by definition Bangladesh is a country where governance is not easy. We have a small land area. We have a huge population. We have natural challenges, but we have enormous potential if we can turn our human resources into a valuable productive asset, which we can do through technology, education and good governance.”

item.title: Grameen HealthTech champion under ‘Inclusion & Community Services’ in BIIN Awards 2026
item.description:
Shukhee, the AI-enabled, patient-centric and interoperable digital healthcare application and community-care ecosystem developed by Grameen HealthTech Limited, has won the Bangladesh ICT & Innovation Network (BIIN) Awards in the "Inclusion & Community Services" category for delivering affordable and continuous healthcare to rural and underserved communities.
Held on October 3 at Brac University Auditorium, the award was received on behalf of Grameen HealthTech by CEO Dr Ahmed Arman Siddiqui; chief business and technology officer Mohammad Solaimun Russell; strategic adviser Mohammad Abul Hossain Bangabashi; chief marketing officer Kingshuk Haque; application tech lead Md Tanvir Hossain; and chief of research, analytics, and customer experience Dr Hossain Md. Al-Amin.
Expressing gratitude to the BIIN organizers and jury board, partner organizations, and the Grameen Group family, Grameen HealthTech CEO Dr Ahmed Armaan Siddiqui said in a statement to the media: "This recognition belongs to every Link Worker, doctor and service recipient who has made Shukhee a part of their lives. Healthcare should not depend on where a person lives. This award will inspire us to bring quality healthcare to every household in Bangladesh."
Shukhee is designed to deliver affordable, accessible and continuous healthcare, particularly for rural, underserved and digitally excluded communities.
It connects patients, doctors, pharmacies, diagnostic centres, hospitals, caregivers, Shukhee Seba Kendro and community-based Shukhee Link Workers through one integrated care pathway.
Its services include 24/7 telemedicine, specialist consultations, digital prescriptions, medicine delivery, home diagnostics, referrals, mental-health support, maternal and child healthcare, and NCD management.
Continuous follow-up is supported by integrated, interoperable Electronic Medical Records (EMR).
An AI-enabled healthcare chatbot provides 24/7 service navigation, preliminary symptom intake, health education, appointment assistance, and medication and follow-up reminders, with seamless escalation to qualified healthcare professionals.
The Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) draws on structured patient histories, clinical observations and real-time vital signs to help doctors identify risk and make guideline-based, evidence-informed decisions.
Through doorstep Link Workers, Shukhee Seba Kendro and connected medical devices, including the Shukhee Sastho Bondhu 6-in-1 Device for real-time health assessment, Shukhee turns every rural household into a connected point of patient-centric care.

item.title: Deputy speaker urges accountability for failure to enforce child laws
item.description:
Deputy Speaker Barrister Kayser Kamal on Sunday stressed the need to ensure proper enforcement of laws to protect children's rights by holding those responsible accountable in case of failure.
“In cases of domestic violence where children are subjected to abuse and exploitation, law enforcement agencies unfortunately become compromised. There is a lack of scrutiny (monitoring) in our country regarding the extent to which executive officials are actually fulfilling their responsibilities,” he said.
The deputy speaker made these remarks at a dialogue titled "What Can We Do to Eliminate Child Labour" arranged by Action for Social Development (ASD) at the KIB Complex in the capital.
Citing that the ministers and MPs are elected for a particular period, while the executive officials remain in charge for a long time, he said the government officials must be held accountable in case of failure to enforce laws.
“Why are we not bringing government officials within the ambit of accountability? They receive their salaries from taxpayers’ money and must be accountable for their responsibilities,” he said.
Talking about child rape, Barrister Kayser Kamal said, unfortunately, this has turned into a social disease. “Why? Because they (children) are the most vulnerable elements and also the worst victims in our society,” he said.
He put emphasis on raising public awareness to overcome this social problem. “If we wish to overcome this situation, the first thing we need is public awareness. The government has a helpline—1098—though many of us may not be aware of it. Why isn't the number 1038 on everyone's lips today? While 999 is widely known, why isn't 1098?
The Deputy Speaker said 12-13% of the 1,400 people killed during the 2024 July Uprising were children.
He called for stronger coordination among Parliament, relevant Ministries, law enforcement agencies and NGOs working on child labour and child rights.
He urged the authorities concerned to ensure that existing laws and government projects related to child protection are properly implemented, saying that laws alone are not enough to protect child rights.
The Deputy Speaker urged participants to pledge not to employ children aged below 14 as domestic workers, saying efforts to eliminate child labour must begin from one's own home. “Let us start from this very room,” he said.
