item.description:
Ten people have been arrested in a case filed over an alleged attempt to seize a house, vandalise property and extort money in Adabor, Dhaka, police said.
Four of the suspects, including two who were injured in police gunfire, were arrested during an overnight operation. Police said they opened fire in self-defence after the suspects allegedly attempted to attack officers with machetes.
The incident took place around 2:30am on Monday in an open area beside a canal behind a playground near Kacha Bazar in Naboday Housing, Adabor.
The two injured suspects were identified as Rajib Howlader, 30, and Sagar, 24. Both sustained gunshot wounds to their legs and were taken to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital for treatment.
The other two arrested during the operation were identified as Shakib, 23, and Rashed, 24.
Adabor police said they launched the operation around 2am based on information about the suspects’ whereabouts. Seven to eight people were present at the scene.
When police attempted to arrest them, the suspects allegedly tried to attack officers with machetes. Police then fired two rounds from a shotgun carried by a constable in self-defence, according to police.
Rajib and Sagar were injured, while the others fled. Police recovered numerous weapons from the scene.
Adabor police station Officer-in-Charge Zahidul Islam said police opened fire after the suspects allegedly attempted to attack them.
“The injured were sent to hospital. Legal action will be taken in connection with the incident,” he said.
The OC said six people had previously been arrested in the case, and the four arrests during the overnight operation brought the total number of suspects arrested to 10.
According to police, Sagar has eight cases filed against him with Adabor and Mohammadpur police stations. Rajib is a named accused in the Babu murder case in Mohammadpur.
Shakib and Rashed each have five cases against them, police said.
On Sunday, a group of 15-20 people allegedly attacked a house in Shyamoli Housing, Adabor, carrying machetes, ramdas and pistols, in an alleged attempt to seize the property.
A case was filed with Adabor police station over the incident.
Police said the two sides had been involved in a longstanding dispute over ownership of the house and that a court case concerning the property is ongoing.

item.title: Gold prices drop further
item.description:
The Bangladesh Jewellers Association (Bajus) has reduced gold prices again, with the price of 22-carat hallmarked gold falling by Tk190 per gram.
Under the new rates, 22-carat gold jewellery will cost Tk19,595 per gram.
The new prices came into effect at 10am on Tuesday.
The Bajus Standing Committee on Pricing and Price Monitoring set the new rates at a meeting at 9am on Tuesday. The decision was announced in a notification signed by the committee’s chairman, Dr Dewan Aminul Islam Shahin.
Under the new rates, 21-carat gold will cost Tk18,715 per gram, while 18-carat gold will cost Tk16,070. Gold sold under the traditional method has been priced at Tk13,130 per gram.
The price of one bhori (11.664 grams) of 22-carat gold now stands at approximately Tk2,28,477. Making charges will be added separately based on the design of the jewellery.
On Monday, September 28, Bajus had set the price of 22-carat gold at Tk19,785 per gram. The latest reduction brings the price down by Tk190 per gram in a single day.
The price had previously been reduced on September 26, when 22-carat gold was priced at Tk19,970 per gram.
Compared with September 26, the price of 22-carat gold has therefore fallen by Tk375 per gram, or approximately Tk4,374 per bhori , in three days.
Bajus has also reduced silver prices.
Under the new rates, 22-carat silver will cost Tk370 per gram, 21-carat silver Tk355, 18-carat silver Tk305 and traditional-method silver Tk230 per gram.
The price of 22-carat silver was Tk385 per gram on September 28, meaning it had fallen by Tk15 per gram in one day.
On September 26, 22-carat silver was priced at Tk415 per gram, representing a decline of Tk45 per gram over three days.
Bajus said making charges will apply separately depending on the design of the jewellery.
However, as VAT is already included in the fixed selling price, it cannot be charged separately to customers.
For exchanges involving old gold jewellery, 12% will be deducted, excluding making charges and the cost of stones. For purchases of old jewellery, the deduction will be 18%.
VAT cannot be deducted separately in either exchange or purchase transactions, according to Bajus.
The new rates will remain in effect at jewellery shops across the country until further notice.
Bajus said the new gold and silver prices were set after considering the overall market situation and a decline in the prices of raw gold and silver.

item.title: Bangladesh Missions abroad go offline due to technical issues with DIP server
item.description:
The government is working to address the technical issues as soon as possible and help the Bangladesh Missions abroad deal with visa processing issues, as the server is currently unavailable.
“Efforts are underway to address the technical issues as soon as possible,” a senior official told UNB on Monday night, noting that due to technical issues with the central system of the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP), Bangladesh, the MRV (Machine Readable Visa) server is currently unavailable.
He said all the Missions abroad are facing the same problem. A visa applicant who applied from a European country told UNB that he submitted his visa application online but has been unable to proceed with the process due to the technical issue.
“Although the system indicated that I would receive an email within 24 hours of submitting the application, I have not received any email so far, while repeated calls have gone unanswered,” said the applicant.
Due to the technical issues, the processing of NVR (No Visa Required (NVR)) and visa applications and the issuance of visas at the Bangladesh Missions abroad are experiencing a temporary delay.
The Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP), Bangladesh, is working to resolve the technical issues and restore the central system at the earliest possible time.
The government has requested the applicants to allow additional time for the processing of their applications and to refrain from making repeated enquiries regarding the status of their applications during this period.
Meanwhile, the Embassy of Bangladesh, Berlin, in an urgent notice, regretted any inconvenience caused and appreciated the patience, understanding and cooperation of all concerned.
Applicants will be informed via the websites and Facebook pages of the Missions abroad once the central system is restored and normal visa services resume.
Another official said the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP) conveyed to the Missions abroad the information regarding the technical issues last week, as it is applicable to all.
The Embassy of Bangladesh in Bangkok, in a public message on Tuesday, said it informed all visa service seekers that, due to a temporary technical issue with the visa server, applicants may experience difficulties in submitting visa applications and/or receiving visa-related services.
The embassy said the concerned technical team is working to resolve the issue as soon as possible.
Applicants have been requested to bear with the temporary inconvenience and, where possible, avoid making urgent travel arrangements dependent on immediate visa processing until the system is fully restored.
The embassy regretted the inconvenience caused and appreciated the patience and understanding of all concerned.

item.title: DB arrests Jamaat MP’s son-in-law over attack on Salman Muqtadir’s studio
item.description:
Detective Branch (DB) of police has arrested Mizanur Rahman, 59, the son-in-law of Jamaat-e-Islami’s Kushtia-2 constituency MP Md Abdul Gafur, in a case filed over an attack on New Guinea Properties in Dhaka’s ECB Chattar area.
Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) DB chief and Additional Commissioner Shafiqul Islam confirmed the arrest to Dhaka Tribune on Tuesday morning.
He said investigators had obtained significant information by questioning those already arrested and that operations were underway to arrest others who may have been involved.
According to the DB chief, Major General (retd) Golam Mahiuuddin Chowdhury and Nazim Uddin, the owner of New Guinea Properties, have been involved in a longstanding dispute over the possession and control of 35 kathas of land.
He said people allegedly acting on behalf of Major General (retd) Golam Mahiuuddin Chowdhury entered the New Guinea Properties premises and vandalised several structures.
The DB chief said an investigation into Mahiuuddin Chowdhury’s alleged involvement was underway and that he would be questioned if necessary. Legal action would be taken if evidence of his involvement is found, he added.
On Monday around 5pm, a DB Gulshan Division team detained Mizanur Rahman from his residence in Dhaka’s West Matikata area, according to AFM Anwar Hossain, deputy commissioner of the DB’s Gulshan Division.
The DB said Mizanur was named accused No 9 in a case filed with Cantonment police station on September 27.
On Saturday night, unidentified individuals attacked New Guinea Properties in the ECB Chattar area.
During the attack, the Brownfish studio of content creator Salman Muqtadir was extensively vandalised and looted. Muqtadir had rented a floor of the New Guinea Properties-owned building and set up his studio there.
Police said the studio was also vandalised during the attack.

item.title: Shama highlights Bangladesh-US education cooperation in California
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam highlighted opportunities to deepen Bangladesh-US cooperation in education, science, research and technology during talks with Arizona State University (ASU) representatives in California.
A Bangladesh delegation led by Prime Minister’s Adviser for Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir met the ASU representatives at the Four Seasons Hotel Silicon Valley on September 27, said a foreign ministry’s press release Tuesday morning.
The talks focused on linking engineering education, research, workforce development, industry and investment to build a semiconductor ecosystem in Bangladesh.
Potential areas of cooperation included microelectronics curricula, faculty training, applied research and partnerships between universities and industry.
State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Boby Hajjaj underscored STEM education and teacher development, while Prime Minister’s Adviser Rehan Asif Asad called for a semiconductor roadmap connecting research and education with investment and commercial use.
Titumir stressed sustainable planning and stronger links between education and industry to turn technology partnerships into skilled jobs, research capacity and investment.
The two sides also explored cooperation with ASU’s University Design Institute on higher education reform.
They discussed developing a memorandum of understanding covering semiconductor education, workforce and faculty development, research and institutional cooperation.
Prime Minister’s Protocol Officer-2 Kamrul Islam, Deputy Press Secretary-1 Md Jahidul Islam, Bangladesh ambassador to the US Tareq Md Ariful Islam, and Consul General in Los Angeles Kazi Muhammad Jabed Iqbal also participated.
Bangladesh’s Consulate General in Los Angeles will facilitate follow-up discussions to identify specific projects and partner institutions, the release said.

item.title: Beyond the bottom line
item.description:
The Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) opened its January spectrum auction, expecting the high-stakes competition typical of vital national infrastructure sales. Instead, the room fell silent.
Grameenphone acquired 10 MHz of the 700 MHz band at the base reserve price of Tk 2,370 crore, Robi withdrew, while Banglalink stayed away from the bidding, leaving 10 MHz of the unsold spectrum to be assigned later to state-owned Teletalk at the same rate.
Failing to attract competition, this transaction left policy-makers with a critical question: How can such an auction dictate the pricing of an upcoming renewal cycle?
The short answer is it cannot . True market value requires viable alternatives where operators bid for expansion, not survival. Spectrum renewal offers no such luxury.
Once a mobile operator anchors its network architecture around a specific band and deploys thousands of base stations, walking away is no longer an option. A renewal price has little to do with market value; it is apparently a reflection of short-term state treasury demands colliding with an operator's inability to walk away without shutting down their business.
This structural disconnect matters as Bangladesh approaches the November renewal of spectrum in the 900 MHz, 1.8 GHz, and 2.1 GHz bands. Data from the GSMA’s 2025 study reveals that Bangladesh’s spectrum costs consume 15.7% of operators’ recurring revenues, much higher than the Asia-Pacific median of 10.4% and the global median of 7.7%.
Macroeconomic modeling suggests that cutting this economic burden to half could unlock $34 billion in cumulative economic benefits by 2035 and a 75% reduction could generate $45bn. These numbers are no prescription to slash prices; rather, they must be weighed against the state’s undeniable fiscal duty to manage a public asset.
At the same time, operators need capital for advanced radios and network upgrades. The real policy challenge is not finding an arbitrary, magic price per megahertz, but ensuring that every megahertz becomes highly productive.
Spectrum productivity is best measured by its capacity for dense urban hubs, wider coverage for rural villages, and reliable network quality during peak hours. Yet, BTRC data exposes a deep structural imbalance in our airwaves.
State-owned Teletalk holds 65.2 MHz for just 6.8 million subscribers, while Grameenphone must squeeze 84.4 million subscribers into 137.4 MHz. Serving remote terrain explains part of this gap, but not all of it.
When rigid frameworks lock spectrum in underutilized silos while urban networks suffer from congestion, the scarcity becomes artificial. Because traffic patterns shift constantly, a band that was adequate five years ago may leave one city congested today while sitting idle in another. If frequency blocks cannot move dynamically to match this shifting public demand, the consumer experience inevitably degrades, and the broader digital economy suffers.
Other nations have long recognized that draining an operator's capital through high upfront spectrum fees may starve the investments needed for network rollouts. Many have shifted toward models that trade immediate financial burdens for guaranteed socio-economic outcomes.
India addressed artificial scarcity by legalizing spectrum trading and sharing , allowing rights to move toward operators facing heavy traffic. Its framework permitted transfers subject to spectrum caps, roll-out obligations, eligibility conditions and a two-year holding period, with a 1% transfer fee.
Similarly, Austria and Colombia tied their low-band spectrum licensing directly to rural coverage, allowing operators to earn explicit fee discounts or convert coverage commitments into cash-equivalent credits. Spain and Canada chose to extend license terms or waive upfront renewal fees where operators could demonstrate minimum population coverage , giving companies the necessary breathing room to amortize massive hardware investments.
The warnings from the global markets should also be watched closely. In its multi-band auction, Pakistan cut reserve prices on legacy bands by more than 50%, yet those bands still drew no bids.
This proved that artificial benchmarks fail to create demand for spectrum that lacks commercial viability. In contrast, Vietnam demonstrates the power of flexible strategic asset pricing; after a failed 2023 auction, it slashed reserve prices by nearly 80%, separating long-term economic utility from the temptation of short-term cash extraction to rapidly achieve roughly 90% 5G coverage by early 2026.
Meanwhile, other regulatory experiments show distinct operational challenges: Austria faced ambiguity over how coverage would be measured. Colombia’s process was criticized for hiding minimum bids in advance while miscalculating rural rollout costs.
Finally, Canada’s model serves as a direct warning; its rigid obligation conditions drove up holding costs without incentivizing efficient use, creating long-term operational inefficiencies after the regulator ignored industry challenges during consultations.
To break out of the cycle of revenue-maximizing deadlocks and deteriorating network quality, Bangladesh needs a pragmatic, forward-looking approach. Rather than exhausting operator liquidity through high upfront hurdles, BTRC can incentivize infrastructure development by recalibrating its renewal fees into a more manageable, back-loaded payment timeline.
Dr Sabbir Ahmad is a tech executive with global experience in digital connectivity, sustainable infrastructure and energy. He is shaping Bangladesh's semiconductor landscape as the CEO of Silicon Array Ltd. Email: sabbir@ieee.org .
